title: Unblocking a foul drain with drain rods
subtitle: Locate the blocked drain, open the inspection chamber, and work the blockage free with a set of drain rods and a plunger or corkscrew head
excerpt: How to unblock a foul drain using drain rods. Covers finding the blocked inspection chamber, screwing the rods together, working the blockage with a plunger or corkscrew head, and flushing the drain clear.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK water industry guidance on drain maintenance (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A brick or precast concrete access point in the garden or driveway that gives access to the underground drain runs. Covered by a metal or plastic access cover. Opening the chamber allows rodding upstream or downstream to clear a blockage.

A section of flexible polypropylene or fibreglass rod (usually 900 mm long) that screws end-to-end to form a longer rod for clearing blocked drains. Heads including a plunger, a corkscrew, and a scraper attach to the leading end. The rods flex around bends but must be turned only clockwise to prevent unscrewing underground.

content.text: A blocked foul drain shows as a slow or non-draining toilet, bath, or gully. The approach is to locate the blockage by checking the
, then work the blockage free with
. This is outdoor work in protective gloves.

Wear protective gloves throughout. Wash hands and any tools thoroughly after finishing. Foul drain water carries harmful bacteria. Do not allow drain overflow to run into a watercourse; it is an offence under the Water Resources Act 1991.

Lift the inspection chamber covers starting nearest the house. The blocked chamber will be full of water or waste; the chamber immediately downstream will be empty or running freely. The blockage is in the drain run between these two chambers.

Screw the plunger or corkscrew head to the first rod. Add rods one at a time as you push the assembly further into the drain. Always turn the rods clockwise as you work; turning anticlockwise unscrews the joints underground, leaving rod sections in the drain, which is a worse problem than the original blockage.

Push the rods toward the blockage with a steady, turning pressure (always clockwise). When the rod meets resistance, apply firm pushes and a slight twist. A plunger head forces water pressure against a soft blockage (fat, paper, roots). A corkscrew head bites into a firm blockage and allows you to pull it back toward the chamber. Flush with a full bucket of water between each push to carry the loosened material downstream.

The blockage has cleared when the standing water level in the chamber drops rapidly. Remove the rods one at a time, unscrewing at the chamber end, not the head end. Pour several buckets of clean water through the drain to flush it thoroughly. Replace the chamber covers and wash down the area.

attrs.symptom: Rods meet an immovable blockage and cannot be pushed further
attrs.cause: A solid root intrusion or a collapsed drain section.
attrs.fix: Try the corkscrew head for a root blockage. A persistent immovable blockage needs a drain survey (CCTV camera inspection) to locate the fault.

attrs.symptom: A rod section comes off and stays in the drain
attrs.cause: Rods were turned anticlockwise at some point during rodding, unscrewing a joint.
attrs.fix: Try a retrieval hook head on the remaining rods to fish out the lost section. If this fails, a drainage contractor with a CCTV unit can locate and retrieve it.
